0588ceaeef4ec889a482.summary: Summary Online co-op comedy horror game for up to four players. Out now in XBOX Game Preview with Steam crossplay. The story of how it got here and what’s next. Ahoy, pirates! We’re RetroStyle Games, a team from Kyiv, Ukraine, and our online co-op horror game Last Pirates: Die Together is out today in XBOX Game Preview on XBOX Series X|S and PC. It has crossplay with Steam! So, a lobby can be half on console and half on PC and still lose their butts together. Up to four pirates land on a cursed island, grab treasure with stretchy arms and drag it back to the ship before the captain’s quota runs out. In practice monsters flip the cart, a monkey begs for coins (bro, we’re broke too), and somebody always wants to tear off a friend’s booty and slap it. Honestly, we had no idea what to write here. We’ve never done anything like this before. Making a game is a thousand small stories, and they won’t fit into 1,000 words. We could just write “butt” a thousand times, but we’d rather share a few favorites, so you get to know the crew behind the booty. Story 1: The Game Jam that Got out of Hand After Ocean Keeper , our pretty serious roguelike, we wanted something much lighter, so in January, 2026 we ran a game jam inside the studio. Once the pirate prototype was playable, the office never got quiet again. Why pirates? Yarr, who doesn’t love pirates?! Loot first, questions later. Every coin counts toward the captain’s quota. Story 2: The Playtest Where the Butt Came off We wanted our pirates to be breakable, so at zero health they snap in half. In one playtest everybody kept trying to stick the bottom half back on, so we coded it, and the revive worked better than anything we had planned. Now monsters bite butts off, crewmates steal them, and a downed pirate comes back when a friend slaps a spare booty onto them. For Steam Next Fest in June we put a giant butt on the beach and asked players to slap it a million times to unlock an update. An average pirate lands about 1,000 slaps in five hours, so we expected it to take a while. But(t)… one crew of four did it alone in seven hours. We were not prepared. Our crew, showing off their best side. Story 3: The Mimic Learns to Talk For a long time the Mimic was our most boring monster: it only copied how a player looked, and we could spot it every time. Then streamers walked straight up to it, sure it was their buddy. Okay, the Mimic works. Time to make it worse. Now each Mimic picks any player in the lobby, copies their skin and borrows short shouts from their voice chat. Two Mimics on the map? Two pirates in the crew have evil twins. Today it’s our favorite monster (not counting the muscle-mice, they’re number one). When the lights go out, hide. Then hide better. 12218893c912e2c16409.summary: This past weekend, the National Atomic Testing Museum in Las Vegas, Nevada (aka, “Old Vegas”) doubled the size of its “World of Fallout” exhibit, which has been open to the public since November 2025. The exhibit juxtaposes recreated objects from the Fallout universe with the real-life artifacts from the nuclear era that inspired the game’s design. Playfully dark satire of Atomic Age retrofuturism and Cold War paranoia has always been a central pillar of the Fallout franchise, making the Atomic Museum a uniquely fitting place to explore the relationship between the games, and now the Prime Video series, and the real-world history that inspired them. One year after its launch, the exhibit has now doubled its footprint with two new galleries, featuring an interactive Overseer’s Desk, a fan-made, full-size Mister Handy robot, on-camera costumes from Season 2 of Prime Video’s “Fallout,” and more. Below are some tips for what to check out in the newly expanded exhibit, and some of our favorite easter eggs tying together the Fallout universe with real-world history. Always Be Scavenging Just like playing a Fallout game, the best way to experience the exhibit is to take your time and pay attention to the little things. Even before reaching the World of Fallout galleries, you can take part in a Fallout Finds, an interactive scavenger hunt throughout the museum that encourages you to track down Fallout-themed items and scan their QR codes. Once you’re in the World of Fallout, be sure to keep scavenging, hidden historical artifacts and supply caches to be found tucked away in certain drawers and cabinets. The Perks of Being a Hacker Again, just like in the games, there are terminals to hack at the new Overseer’s Desk. Succeed, and you’ll get to read strange and spooky real-life anecdotes from the long history of the Nevada Test Site. Even if you’re a Fallout hacking master and have no trouble cracking the code, be sure to fail deliberately … you’ll want to see the warning that pops up Signed Work The exhibit features replicas of the in-game signs for New Vegas and the Lucky 38 casino, complete with classic Vegas neon. These were created in partnership with the University of Nevada, Las Vegas by students and staff in its Entertainment, Engineering, and Design program, providing what was no doubt a fun and valuable hands-on learning experience. Fact or Fiction One of the exhibit’s main elements juxtaposes real historical objects, like posters and pulp books, with their fictional Fallout equivalents. You might be surprised at how little Fallout exaggerates some parts of ’50s material culture. Hands Off Mister Handy Visitors to the exhibit are greeted by a life-size Mister Handy robot replica, created by fan fabricator, Dragonfoot3D, who also made the Deathclaw and terminal replicas.. Unlike some other parts of the exhibit, this unique museum piece is not to be touched, and his eyes will react threateningly if you get too close, to underline the point. 250c5c3e15252ea6831a.summary: In Ice Cream Simulator , you can leave a customer waiting, go away for an hour, and come back to find them still standing there, ready to order. They have nowhere more important to be. They have chosen ice cream. We respect that. Their infinite patience is one of our most deliberate design decisions. We wanted to capture the pleasure of running your own ice cream shop while giving you time to enjoy it. Real life already supplies plenty of deadlines. We didn’t feel the need to put another one on a cone. It Started with a Scoop Our inspiration was simple: we love ice cream. We also hadn’t seen many games explore running an ice cream shop in the way we imagined. We wanted to create something cozy and hands-on, where you could turn your love of dessert into a business of your own. The design challenge was giving that simple idea enough depth to keep you interested, while protecting the relaxed atmosphere that made us want to build it. Hold the Stress We built the shop around a daily rhythm. During the day, you serve ice cream with different toppings and sauces, along with milkshakes. At night, you prepare for the days ahead. That rhythm gives you both sides of the experience: the satisfaction of serving an order and the preparation that makes tomorrow’s orders possible. But serving customers can easily become a game about speed. We wanted you to settle into the routine, so we gave customers unlimited patience. Take your time with an order. Step away if you need to. Your customer will remain impressively committed to dessert. For us, this was a way to put the emphasis on decisions about the business. You have time to think about what you are building, which leads to the question at the heart of the game: what kind of shop do you want to run? Three Customers, Three Priorities We designed three customer groups to give that question a meaningful answer. Elite customers want the best ice cream and don’t care about the price. They are here for quality, and your ingredient budget is about to hear about it. Office customers look for a balance between price and quality. They appreciate good ice cream, but they would also appreciate the numbers making sense. Casual customers care most about affordability. Premium ingredients are not the selling point for them. A reasonably priced ice cream is. Those differences are why we wanted you to choose between cheaper and more premium ingredients. Keeping costs low can support a shop aimed at casual customers. Spending more on quality can support one designed to attract elite customers. We wanted both approaches to have a purpose. Buying the most expensive ingredients should be a decision that fits your business, rather than an automatic answer to every problem. Your Shop, Your Style Once you start thinking about your audience, the walls become surprisingly relevant. Our attractiveness attribute connects the appearance of your shop with the customers it attracts. Renovating the floors, walls, and ceiling becomes part of your business strategy. 39bdb9361a56de520bdb.summary: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is the first Castlevania game since 2008. 18 years had to pass for a brand-new title in the series to come out. And no, I’m not counting Lords of Shadow . While I’m happy for those that enjoy the newest Castlevania romp, it’s not what I think about when I picture the series. If you were to ask me what defines a Castlevania game, I’d say it’s either the classic arcade-style original games, or the Koji Igarashi-led games. In the hypothetical sliding scale between Metroid and Castlevania , it seems like Belmont’s Curse veers closer to the former. In fact, I’d venture to say that there are too many Metroidvania games in the style of Metroid , and not nearly enough similar to the Igarashi-led Castlevania games. When I think of Metroidvania in the Castlevania “Igavania” style, I think of games like Ender Lilies and Ender Magnolia , Team Ladybug’s Record of Lodoss War: Deedlit in Wonder Labyrinth and Blade Chimera , and of course, Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night . I’m sure there are a few more, but even so, the list isn’t very long. What differentiates these games different from the likes of Hollow Knight or Blasphemous is a heavier emphasis on RPG elements, varied weapons and equipment, different spells and abilities, and a design ethos more focused on fighting hordes of enemies, rather than focusing on moment-to-moment, deliberate and challenging enemy encounters. Image via Konami By now it’s probably obvious that I gravitate towards the Castlevania side of things. However, I’ve officially run out of games in that style to play. I could boot up a plethora of other Metroidvania games, sure. But games that draw specifically from the style that originated with Castlevania: Symphony of the Night ? I’m afraid it’s looking dire. And I get it. What I’m asking for is a fundamentally different design style from what’s popular in the genre nowadays. The Igavania games are, usually, experiences where the player has a lot more control over the pacing of enemy encounters. It’s pretty easy to cheese through a Symphony of the Night or Bloodstained , get a particular weapon drop and start mowing down enemies. What’s more popular nowadays is the FromSoft style of challenge and curated fights. This style marries well with the non-linear exploration of the genre, but fundamentally changes how to approach combat and bosses, compared to how fast one can decimate bosses in Castlevania or adjacent games. Even the aforementioned Ender Lilies and Ender Magnolia are skirting the line between Igavania and Soulslike at times. The same goes for a lot of other side-scrolling action games, like Salt and Sanctuary , The Last Faith , or Mandragora: Whispers of the Witch Tree . While these are interesting games, it’s not exactly what I’m looking for in this space either. Image via Team Cherry Recent gaming trends have drastically changed the Metroidvania, with games like Hollow Knight and Dark Souls influencing how the genre plays. Even Metroid Dread boasts a parry and an increase in challenge compared to the rest of the series. 9671751db164a1d6f62d.summary: FuRyu is one of those companies where you tend to know what their games might be like before they drop as a result of the track record. They can absolutely be fun and memorable, but we know they’re more likely to be average and a little flawed than some AAA, once-in-a-lifetime, must-play. But usually about once a year or so, we’ll see an absolute banger in the roster, and CRYMELIGHT is it. It isn’t a perfect roguelike, but its Hades and Cult of the Lamb approach to dungeon-crawling combat, Poker hand approach to ability upgrades, and troubled characters combine into something worth playing. It also fits well within the established CRY series alongside CRYSTAR and CRYMACHINA . CRYMELIGHT is set in Wonderland, a purgatory where troubled sinners compete in a death game based on Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland for a chance at freedom if they defeat the Queen. Our adventure begins with a young woman in a blue and white dress facing that final boss. As she’s about to win, she’s defeated. Time then rewinds to a point at which we see a blue butterfly floating through the Queen’s gardens. A voice warns that if she loses her sense of self, she’ll be targeted b the Card Soldiers and eliminated. It seems she could falter until she sees another, colorless butterfly about to suffer the same fate. She defends them, then develops a body again and gains a CRYME weapon. White Rabbit then appears a a guide and declares the nameless girl, who is suffering from amnesia and now given the moniker Alice, a challenger in the death game. Though she suggests abandoning and destroying the other butterfly, Alice claims she owes her one and is her “plus one.” That girl too, who also can’t remember who she is, develops a sense of self and becomes Mary. From there, we jump into solid gameplay loop. The Tea Party Hall hub in Wonderland features a table section with March where you can unlock story scenes of the four challengers Alice, Cheshire, March, and Mad, as well as Mary, that offer insights into who they were in the past and are now. The Tailor lets you upgrade Alice’s weapons and equip accessories. At the Confessional, you can use points earned from dungeon runs to unlock/upgrade abilities (like a revival) and upgrade stats. You can also check in with Cheshire at the library to see past story scenes and segments. It’s a way to relax and prepare for runs, while also perhaps gaining more insights into individuals. Heading out through the doors to Wonderland sends you through different realms toward the Queen’s castle. In typical roguelike fashion, we’re presented with a map with nodes and shown what the “reward” might be for selecting it. This could range from things like additional cards that bolster your attacks and moveset, Skill acquisition, and currency for areas like the Tailor or Wonderland shop. Selecting nodes will send you either into a small stage with a set number of enemies or a shop run by White Rabbit. Once you defeat all of the foes, you get your reward, are sent back to the map, and continue until you reach that region’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland -themed boss. a42e3d892bb4f4ad1205.summary: What if a sky-spanning Colossus didn’t just loom overhead as a static backdrop, but actively listened and responded to your every gunshot? That’s the core question driving our upcoming fifth season, Dissonant Resonance, free to play and launching globally on November 18. Today, I want to take you behind the scenes to share how we are turning sound and emotion into your greatest weapons – and your biggest threats. New weird meets a symphony of dread Once Human thrives on the New Weird design philosophy – taking the familiar and twisting it into a nightmare. For Season 5, we wanted to apply this philosophy not just to the visuals, but to the audio itself. As we realized players always take background music for granted, we decided to weaponize it. Inspired by the cathedral pipe organ, a human symbol of sanctity and solemnity, and through the lens of the New Weird, we distorted this familiar object into a cosmic, biomechanical monstrosity: What if the music wasn’t just playing in your headset, but was the literal breathing and judgment of a cosmic monstrosity watching your every move? This idea birthed the Sky Living-Machine Colossus. By merging the sacred with the grotesque, this massive pipe-organ titan transforms the very rhythm of the world into an active, weaponized mechanic. Emotion zones & rhythmic gunplay To ground this massive concept in actual gameplay, we’ve warped the open world with four distinct Emotion Zones: Joy, Anger, Sorrow, and Fear. In these erratic regions, your arsenal becomes an instrument. Defeating enemies scatters musical notes across the battlefield. By shooting these notes, you not only trigger pitch-tuned audio to improvise your own battle rhythms, but also collect them to purify dissonant, corrupted scores. Once these notes are rearranged into harmonious melodies, the scores grant your squad powerful rewards. We’ve been keeping a secret under wraps at Imprnt Studios and Silver Lining Interactive, and we can finally let the dog out of the bag: Hounded is heading to PS5 in 2027. Get ready to step into the paws of a brave (and incredibly adorable) Border Collie, Duke, as you help him search for his lost master in an epic journey across the conflict-torn world of Anglodia. Hounded has been in development for just over two years, and in that time we’ve been hard at work developing our very own Motion Matching system for our main character. Along with this exciting announcement, we wanted to show you what making our passion project actually looks like behind the scenes. So, we put together our very first dev diary with a full look into how the sausage (or kibble?) gets made. Have you ever wondered how you make a dog communicate through animation? Or what a realistic quadruped animation made from scratch looks like before it lands on your screen? We’re tackling all of that and more, while introducing the little guy who started this entire journey: Duke. Check it out. Play Video A dog story – who is Duke? Duke is a young, clumsy, yet loyal Border Collie. He lives in the world of Anglodia – a flintlock fantasy inspired Britain in the late 18th century. It is a beautiful and mythical land filled with mysterious technology that is coming apart at the seams under tyrannical rule. However, Duke’s interests lie outside of politics and the brewing rebellion against the crown… His master, Artemys Fletcher – a secretive key player in the resistance, has vanished. Duke’s home has been torn apart by the regime and the only thing that matters now is finding his master. Building a border collie from the paws up Here’s the thing about four-legged protagonists: you can’t just reskin a two-legged skeleton and call it a day. In our earliest test builds, Duke moved like a clunky wooden table with paws. It felt terrible—Border Collies have this iconic, low-slung energy that looks like they are about to run at all times. To bring this into reality in Unreal Engine, we decided to animate all of Duke’s movement by hand, using a handcrafted Motion Matching system. Eventually, we were able to set it up so that it pulls from a library of animations based on real-world references, selects the most appropriate animation for the movement, and smooths out the whole process (for the dev team and for the players). What does the dog say? Giving Duke a good expressive range has easily been one of the biggest creative mountains our narrative and animation teams had to climb. Games like Hello Kitty Island Adventure helped, given how many show up as island residents and visitors. With Hello Kitty Party Land, a Mario Party style party game with minigames that dig into the archives, we see a lot more variety. However, while it’s nice to see such a large cast, the game itself is geared more towards kids under the age of 10 and leaves older fans out. While I do believe Hello Kitty Party Land is both overly easy and simplistic in general, there’s significant effort put in to making it feel unique and offer more than just games to play. When it begins, you get to create a custom avatar and deck them out in clothes inspired by Sanrio characters and their aesthetics. You start with 1000 gold, enough to pull together a solid outfit, with more rewarded for playing. Once you decide to start a game, there are quite a few options too. Between one and four players can play locally solo, and there is an online option for two to four people. (The connection seemed solid both times I tried.) It is also possible to choose from minigame difficulty levels ranging from Easy to Super Hard, though if everyone playing is at or over the age of 10 I think I’d recommend considering Super Hard to start. Especially since a big part of the overall experience involves working together to win. As for playing games, there are essentially two options to jump into things in the Game Park section of Hello Kitty Party Land . One is to head to Minigame Corner. That’s where you can specifically play the 45 minigames piecemeal outside of the board games included in the collection. The receptionist lets you go through the Blooming Flower Festival, Sparkling Neon Night, and Tropical Twilight board games. These are the short, Mario Party style boards in Hello Kitty Party Land that involve collecting flowers, sparks, or droplets to help characters with events tied to each one. These are quite short and usually last under an hour, with Petit Game Shop Spaces, Petit Game Challenge Spaces, Minigame Spaces, Item Spaces, and Delivery Spaces to land on. The good part of these boards in Hello Kitty Party Land is each one features one of the Sanrio characters we might not know as well as the star. Blooming Flower Festival involves Marron Cream the bunny trying to prepare an event. Sparkling Neon Night’s stars are the three Oni kids Goropikadon who can’t perform without enough electricity. Tropical Twilight tags in WeAreDinosaurs’ Tiran the T-rex gathering water to grow fruit for friends. That, paired with all boards being short, is handy for younger kids with attention spans that might not withstand Mario Party ’s lengthy games or more bloodthirsty minigames. e45d1c2f8fc9c018b23f.summary: During the early hours of Grand Theft Auto VI , I was walking near a bowling alley in an interstate area. Playing as Lucia, I overheard chatter about an ongoing drug operation inside. I desperately needed money, so I engaged in some tomfoolery. I took a shotgun from my car, approached the guard, and opened fire at their knees, taking them down without killing them. I took as much loot with me as I could from the wild shootout and eventually found a locked safe and some explosives nearby. You can imagine what I did next. It didn’t take long until the police surrounded the bowling alley. There was no easy way out. I had been greedy, took too long, and had to deal with my choices. As the police entered the building, another shootout between the gang members and the cops ensued. That was my cue. I climbed a ladder to the roof, jumped to the street, and drove an unlocked motorbike as fast as I could, hoping the cops wouldn’t recognize me. It was as if I had never been there, and I was a handful grand richer in GTA VI . This is just one example of the dozens of situations I got into over 83 hours in Leonida. However, if I told you that some of my other favorite moments in GTA VI involved setting up some drywall as Jason and moving a coffee table, you’d probably look at me funny. Grand Theft Auto VI is a game of contrasts. Image via Rockstar GTA VI shares a lot in common with Red Dead Redemption 2 , but it’s in how these two games differ that the former shines. While I appreciate RDR2 , it features a very stark divide between what you can do in its world with those systems and how the main story missions take place. GTA VI features bombastic set pieces, car pursuits, and scripted sequences aplenty, especially in the later chapters. The game suffers a bit as it moves into the second half, where these more linear missions and set pieces take place. Especially considering the length of it. But GTA VI also constantly required me to engage with the open world and these granular, interactive systems in order to advance the story. During one early story mission, Jason and Lucia need to rob a few stores to get some cash, but you don’t need to hit all of them. Which ones I robbed and how I went about it was all up to me. Some I managed to hit clean and fast, with the cops unable to track me. With others, I failed to find and eliminate CCTV recordings. I got in trouble with the law and had to skulk around the shadows, find the correct car to steal, and wait for an opportunity to approach the nearest clothing store to change my appearance. Images via Rockstar The usual freedom is also met with a level of friction and limitations that creates fascinating opportunities in GTA VI . These limitations made me engage with systems that I’d otherwise not try, such as public transport and taxis, and I’d always make sure my car was in top shape and with a full tank. fb46f33316f5ad3aebd0.summary: Nissin has revealed that it is working with Square Enix to launch a Dragon Quest crossover campaign that features a blanket modeled after Liquid Metal Slime. The former has also opened a pre-order page on its website. This campaign features a special set that people will have to buy with a tax-inclusive price tag of ¥4,990 (~$31.30). In addition to the blanket, the set will come with two packs each of all four Nissin Raoh instant noodle flavors. Rounding out this set will be three packs of the Nissin Maoh crossover noodles. This product is named after a wordplay on Nissin Raoh by replacing a letter to turn it into Maoh (Demon Lord). It will also include chili powder that produces a spiciness level of 4 out of 5. Image courtesy of Square Enix and Nissin Nissin will close pre-orders for the instant noodle set with Liquid Metal Slime Blanket when it reaches the allocated quota. The company will ship the orders in two batches in mid-December 2026 and late April 2027, respectively. Square Enix is helping Nissin manage this crossover campaign, as the former is also promoting Dragon Quest Monsters: The Withered World , which is coming out on December 3, 2026.

To pick up where you left off, someone needs to download the PC version of Nekopara Sekai Connect from Steam.
